content.text: What Is Butlerian Jihad? — full essay import
content.html:
What Is Butlerian Jihad?

I kept seeing this meme on Twitter.

I haven't read Dune(Will I read it? Probably not.) But the phrase stuck. Butlerian Jihad. 

It sounded like something that mattered—something old and violent and strange. Two words that shouldn't be together, creating friction, excitement, and curiosity every time I encountered them.

While a formal inquiry[a]/enquiry might start with the phrase itself, I thought it might be a fun exercise to break down the words first and then hopefully piece together what they might mean to me.

Let's start with the first word. Not "Butlerian" just "Butler."

What is a butler? Who is a butler?

The contemporary image is familiar enough: a man in formal attire answering the door of a grand house, managing household staff, serving at table. Dignified. Deferential. The archetypal English servant. (Oh, Master Bruce.)

The English "butler" arrived through Middle English (buteler) from Anglo-French butuiller and Old French boteillier. The Old French meant "cup-bearer, butler, officer in charge of wine," derived from boteille—wine vessel, bottle. That French word descended from Medieval Latin butticula, a diminutive of buttis, meaning cask.

A butler was a bottle-man.

Someone who handled wine containers. The word traces it clearly: Butler reflects "the position's original function as chief servant in charge of wine."

Wine was valuable. Guarding it required trust. Trust led to status. Over centuries, the bottle-man rose. By the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the butler had become the senior male servant in the grandest households. In the European Middle Ages the title "meant precisely this, but in time it came to mean an official of the crown, who nominally had charge of the wine but who in fact was a person of high rank."

What began with bottles ended with authority.
Proximity to precious things -> power

Now let’s move on to the second word.

Jihad arrives in English with enormous baggage. Most Western listeners hear it and think: holy war, terrorism, religious violence. The word has been weaponized—by extremists who claim it and by commentators who fear it.

Jihad (جِهَاد) derives from the Arabic root j-h-d (ج-ه-د). The root meaning: to strive, to exert effort, to struggle. The Encyclopædia Britannica defines it as "a meritorious struggle or effort" and notes that "it has often been erroneously translated in the West as 'holy war.'"

The word appears throughout the Quran, and its meanings vary by context. During the Meccan period of Muhammad's prophecy, the emphasis was on internal struggle—sabr, patient forbearance in the face of hardship. The Quran speaks of "striving in the path of God" through non-violent means: speaking truth, living righteously, resisting one's own base impulses.

Islamic tradition developed a distinction. The greater jihad (al-jihad al-akbar) refers to the internal spiritual struggle against one's own weaknesses—the ego, selfish desires, moral failings. The lesser jihad (al-jihad al-asghar) refers to external struggle, including but not limited to armed conflict under strict conditions.

This distinction appears in a famous (if contested) hadith: upon returning from battle, the Prophet told his companions, "You have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad." When asked what the greater jihad was, he replied: "A person's jihad against his desires."

The scholar Reuven Firestone puts it directly: "The semantic meaning of the Arabic term jihad has no relation to holy war or even war in general."

In Modern Standard Arabic, jihad is used for struggles both religious and secular. It appears as a given name—for boys and girls—meaning "one who strives."

So: jihad at its root is not about violence. It's about effort. Striving. The hard work of becoming better—whether that work is internal or external, peaceful or, in limited circumstances, martial.

I think I'm kinda getting comfortable addressing the strange adjectival form.

"Butlerian" follows the pattern of other philosophical adjectives: Hegelian, Kantian, Darwinian, Freudian, my friend Ian. (I know none of these philosophies and will probably break myself trying to understand them.) The "-ian" suffix transforms a proper name into a body of thought, a school, a movement. It implies disciples and debates, texts and traditions.

When you say "Hegelian dialectic," you're referencing a system derived from Hegel. When you say "Darwinian evolution," you're invoking Darwin's framework. The suffix signals significance: this person's ideas mattered enough to become an adjective.

"Butlerian" does the same work—but the name it modifies is so ordinary. Butler. A common English surname. The kind of name you'd find on a brass plaque outside a solicitor's office in places that end with shire. And I think that's part of why the phrase works. "Butlerian" sounds like it should describe something dry and academic. A Butlerian analysis of household management. Butlerian principles of wine service.

Then it collides with "Jihad."

Let's try to say it aloud: Butlerian Jihad.

Bu-TLE-ri-an. Ji-HAD.

A jihad named after someone called Butler? Who was Butler? What kind of struggle was this? Why does something that sounds like a committee meeting also sound like a holy war?

The phrase refuses to explain itself. It names without narrating.

My findings led me to Dune, Herbert’s magnum opus. The term appears in its glossary:

JIHAD, BUTLERIAN: (see also Great Revolt) — the crusade against computers, thinking machines, and conscious robots begun in 201 B.G. and concluded in 108 B.G. Its chief commandment remains in the O.C. Bible as "Thou shalt not make a machine in the likeness of a human mind."

The novel is set roughly 20,000 years in the future. The Butlerian Jihad occurred 10,000 years before the story begins—ancient history even to characters living in an unimaginably distant future. Herbert's universe contains no computers, no artificial intelligence, no robots. This absence shapes everything: specialized humans called Mentats are trained to perform complex calculations; the Spacing Guild develops prescient navigators to pilot ships; the Bene Gesserit sisterhood cultivates advanced mental and physical disciplines.

All of this exists because the machines are gone.

Herbert never fully narrated the Jihad in his novels. He gave us the aftermath and let us infer the causes. But the name itself points somewhere interesting.

Which Butler?

Literary scholars have long suspected that Herbert named the Jihad after Samuel Butler, an English writer who lived from 1835 to 1902.

In 1863—four years after Darwin published On the Origin of Species—Butler wrote a letter to a New Zealand newspaper titled "Darwin among the Machines." Writing under the pseudonym Cellarius, Butler raised the possibility that machines were a kind of "mechanical life" undergoing constant evolution:

We refer to the question: What sort of creature man's next successor in the supremacy of the earth is likely to be. We have often heard this debated; but it appears to us that we are ourselves creating our own successors; we are daily adding to the beauty and delicacy of their physical organisation; we are daily giving them greater power and supplying by all sorts of ingenious contrivances that self-regulating, self-acting power which will be to them what intellect has been to the human race.

Butler developed this idea into "The Book of the Machines," three chapters of his 1872 satirical novel Erewhon. The fictional Erewhonians, fearing that machines might evolve to dominate humanity, had destroyed all mechanical inventions developed in the preceding 271 years.

Butler's Erewhonians ban recent machines. The Victorian satirist becomes, in Herbert's hands, something like a prophet.

Herbert never confirmed this connection. In the Dune Encyclopedia (1984)—compiled by Willis E. McNelly with Herbert's approval—an in-universe explanation emerged: the Jihad was named after a woman called Jehanne Butler, whose fetus was forcibly aborted by an AI medical system, sparking the revolt. Herbert wrote in the foreword that he gave the encyclopedia his "delighted approval" but would "hold my own counsel on some of the issues."

That ambiguity is probably deliberate. Or lazy. Herbert maybe loved layered meanings. Who doesn't love obscurity masked as mystery?

In God Emperor of Dune (1981), the character Leto II says: "The target of the Jihad was a machine-attitude as much as the machines. Humans had set those machines to usurp our sense of beauty, our necessary selfdom out of which we make living judgments."

The key phrase: machine-attitude.

The Jihad was not primarily about machines becoming conscious and rebelling. It was about what happened to humans who outsourced their cognition. They stopped making "living judgments." They surrendered the mess of being human—intuition, error, beauty, ambiguity—to systems that optimized, calculated, and decided on their behalf.

In the opening chapter of Dune (1965), the Reverend Mother Gaius Helen Mohiam tells the young protagonist: "Once, men turned their thinking over to machines in the hope that this would set them free. But that only permitted other men with machines to enslave them."

The danger wasn't artificial intelligence. The danger was the humans who wielded it.

Let’s get back to the meme: "Thou shalt not make a machine in the likeness of a human mind."

This is not a prohibition on all technology. Herbert's universe still has aircraft, weapons, medical devices, elaborate machinery. What is forbidden is a specific category: machines that think as humans think.

Why?

The commandment assumes something about human minds worth protecting. Call it agency, or dignity, or capacity for meaning-making.

"Likeness" is a strange word here. It doesn't mean "identical to." A portrait is made in the likeness of a face, but it is not a face. A statue is made in the likeness of a body. A map is made in the likeness of a territory. Likeness implies representation. The prohibition is not against machines that match human cognition, but against machines that represent it—that offer themselves as images of what thinking is.

If you can build a machine that thinks like a human, you have implicitly claimed to understand what human thinking is. You have reduced the mind to a mechanism. And once reduced, it can be replicated, scaled, optimized, controlled.

The Butlerian Jihad was, in this reading, a refusal to be understood completely. A declaration that human minds are not fully formalizable. That there is something in us that resists reduction to process.

Here's where I turn the inquiry toward the present.

We talk often about the danger of anthropomorphizing machines—projecting human qualities onto non-human things. We say the computer "wants" something, or "knows" something, or is "thinking." We treat the machine as if it were a person.

The danger is this: when you call a language model "intelligent" or say it "understands," you are making it in the likeness of a mind. You are claiming the model represents something real about cognition. And once that representation is accepted, it becomes normative. The model becomes the standard against which human thinking is measured.

Every time you say a machine "thinks," you compress what thinking means. Every time you say it "knows," you flatten what knowledge involves. Every time you say it "wants," you simplify what desire entails. The machine cannot object. It accepts whatever words you use. And slowly, the words lose their weight.

But the Butlerian Jihad points to the inverse danger: mechanomorphization.This is when we project machine qualities onto humans. We say people are "programmed" by their upbringing, or "wired" to behave a certain way, or running "mental software." We treat the person as if they were a machine.

Probably Herbert's fear was not that machines would become human. It was that humans would become machines.

We would internalize the logic of optimization, would stop tolerating inefficiency and ambiguity, would come to see their own minds as systems to be debugged rather than lives to be lived.

The Jihad destroyed the thinking machines. But its deeper purpose was to destroy the idea that thinking is just machinery.

Not because the machine will suffer. But because you might forget what the likeness was supposed to represent.

Uncertainty Meter:
I should be honest about the other positions on this spectrum.

There's an accelerationist counter-position where If we can build machines that think like humans, maybe that reveals something true about thinking. Maybe cognition was always reducible to process.

If thought can be formalized, formalize it. If intelligence can be scaled, scale it. The machine doesn't diminish the human; it reveals what the human always was.

The silicon mind doesn't diminish the carbon one; it clarifies it. It was a substrate-independent pattern, and now we could prove it.

While I understand the arguments on both sides and can see the horizon for both ends,I tend to lean a bit towards Herbert's framing.

The Jihad wasn't fought because machines could think. It was fought because humans stopped thinking—stopped making what Leto II called "living judgments." The danger wasn't that minds could be replicated. The danger was that the replication made the thinker feel redundant. The machine-attitude doesn't threaten genius. It threatens the ordinary human work of receiving ideas, sitting with them, passing them on as something slightly transformed. That's what "living judgments" meant,not some pristine originality, but presence. It threatens participation. The living act of borrowing, struggling, misunderstanding, building.

Dedicated to Aditya Prasad,Sky and Groundless Alignment

[a]"Enquiry" relates to the Old French enquerre—to ask about, to explore—while "inquiry" comes from Latin inquirere—to seek into. I like the open-ended version more.hence the order with i first and e later

content.text: Innocence — an exploration of preserving the wild spirit within civilization.
content.html:
Innocence

The deal we make with civilization. You get safety, structure, accumulated knowledge, the benefits of cooperation at scale. In exchange, you give up something. Something that lives fully in children, dims in most adults, and survives only in the people we later call geniuses or artists or, sometimes, saints.

I want to be careful here. This is not a piece about children. It is about something in us. Something that children have access to naturally, before it gets trained out of them, but something that belongs to the structure of the psyche itself. Call it the wild spirit. Call it original nature. Call it innocence, if you understand that word to mean not naivete but a kind of directness, a capacity to see before knowing what you are supposed to see.

Visakan Veerasamy wrote something I keep returning to:

"The handful of people that we call geniuses are typically those who have protected the wild spirit of their inner-child-self into adulthood, fending off good-intentioned domestication. I believe we could have 1000x more geniuses if we took children seriously."

The phrase that catches me is "good-intentioned domestication." Not cruelty. Not neglect. Good intentions. Chip by chip, the environment shapes what was once shapeless.

But what is this spirit?

Every wisdom tradition I can find points toward a similar recognition: There is an original quality in us.

For this enquiry, I’ve been looking especially at Eastern sources — Taoist, Buddhist, Vedantic — partly because they hold this insight more centrally, and partly because the Western conversation about childhood and innocence often gets sentimental in ways that obscure what’s actually being pointed at.

The Taoists called it pu, the uncarved block. The character literally means wood that has not been cut. Before you carve wood into a cup, it could become anything. After, it can only be a cup. Original nature contains limitless potential. Conditioning narrows us into specific shapes.

But Lao Tzu did not tell people to remain uncarved. That is not possible. Life carves you. Experience shapes you. You become a particular person with particular knowledge and particular ways of seeing. The instruction was different: "The sage knows the utensils, yet keeps to the block." (Tao Te Ching, Chapter 28)

Jung approached this from a different direction but arrived at the same place. He wrote about the Divine Child archetype. Not a stage of life but a pattern in the psyche. A symbol of potential, futurity, the possibility of renewal. (The Psychology of the Child Archetype, 1940)

Jung was careful to distinguish the archetypal child from any actual child.

The Divine Child represents, Jung wrote, "both beginning and end, an initial and a terminal creature." He wrote of the archetype as renatus in novam infantiam: reborn into a new childhood.

What does this mean psychologically? The child symbolizes what exceeds consciousness in both directions. Behind us lies the pre-conscious — the unconscious state of earliest childhood, before we learned to partition the world into names and categories. Ahead of us lies what Jung called the post-conscious — not literal life after death, but an anticipation of wholeness that our current awareness cannot yet contain.

This is Jung's crucial point: wholeness is never contained within consciousness. It includes the indefinite and indefinable extent of the unconscious as well.

There is a shadow here. Jung called it the puer aeternus, the eternal youth. This is the person who refuses to grow up. Who lives a provisional life, always waiting for the real thing to begin. Who flees commitment and responsibility and depth. Peter Pan. The eternal student. The middle-aged man still finding himself. This is not what I mean by innocence. This is its counterfeit.

But Jung identified something else, which he called the "higher puer." This is not the adult who refuses maturity. It is the quality of youth that emerges from maturity. Not instead of development but through it. "The boy who is born from the maturity of the adult man," Jung wrote, "and not the unconscious child we would like to remain."

Christ said: "Except ye become as little children, ye shall not enter the kingdom of heaven." (Matthew 18:3) Read through Jung, this means something radical. The childlike quality that grants entry is not what we start with. It is what we arrive at. It is not behind us but ahead.

Jung articulated this as a psychologist, through concepts. But other traditions built the same structure into the body, into practice, into the slow work of mastery through embodiment.

The Japanese martial arts tradition encodes this understanding in its deepest structure.

In the first stage of mastery, Shu, you protect and obey. You learn the forms exactly as the master teaches them. You do not question. You do not improvise. You copy faithfully, even when you do not understand.

In the second stage, Ha, you break and diverge. You question the teachings. You experiment. You begin to understand why the forms are the way they are, which means you also begin to see their limitations. You integrate learning from other sources. You develop your own insights.

In the third stage, Ri, you transcend and separate. You act from intuition. The forms have become so internalized that you no longer need to think about them. You develop your own expression. In some sense, you become a new source.

Here is what matters: the third stage looks like the first stage from the outside. The master's simplicity resembles the beginner's simplicity. But it contains everything the beginner lacks. Bruce Lee put it this way: "Before I studied the art, a punch was just a punch, a kick was just a kick. After I studied the art, a punch was no longer a punch, a kick was no longer a kick. Now I understand the art, and a punch is just a punch, a kick is just a kick."

The Vedantic tradition names this same arc. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, the sage Yajnavalkya speaks of three movements: Shravanam, Mananam, Nididhyasana.

Shravanam is hearing. Mananam is reflection and Nididhyasana is something like absorption, or dwelling. You sit with what you have understood until the separation between knower and known dissolves. The teaching is no longer something you possess. It is something you have become.

What prevents this transformation? What keeps us carved into cups rather than returning to the block?

Russell wrote in 1932 that modern people think everything ought to be done for the sake of something else, never for its own sake. He called this the cult of efficiency.

This is where domestication does its work: not by forbidding joy but by making it instrumental. Rest becomes recovery for more work. Hobbies become networking opportunities. Every hour must answer for itself.

The wild spirit refuses this bargain. It learns because learning is interesting. It talks because talking is happening. Curiosity is not a means to an end but the thing itself.

Civilizations that lose access to this quality lose their connection to renewal. They become efficient at perpetuating themselves but incapable of genuine novelty. They optimize for metrics that have long since disconnected from anything that matters.

This wild nature does not mean regression or primitivism. It means integration of vital energies within civilization. It means refusing over-domestication while also refusing to flee into the woods. It means being in contact with the part of yourself that existed before you learned all the rules about who you were supposed to be.

I have been thinking about what it means to have Innocence as something to protect.

To protect it in myself. The capacity to see freshly. The willingness to ask the obvious question. The ability to do something for its own sake, without justification, without instrumentalizing it into usefulness.

If this is something to protect, then protecting it is not passive. You do not protect it by building walls. You protect it by building skill. By going so far into civilization's games that you come out the other side. By learning the rules so completely that they become tools rather than constraints.

It is not protected by retreating from civilization or refusing its demands. It is protected by learning how to move inside its machinery without being entirely claimed by it. By taking on forms, responsibilities, commitments and still reserving, somewhere, the freedom to ask the naive question, to follow the pointless curiosity, to let a moment be for itself and not for anything beyond itself.

So the work is strangely ordinary. You answer emails. You pay bills. You learn the rules of the systems you are entangled with. And, every so often, you notice that for a breath or two you are simply here: looking at a face, or a tree, or a cracked mug, with the unprejudiced attention of someone who has not yet decided what it is worth.

I don't know if innocence can be built. The phrase feels wrong. It's more like: these practices poke holes in something. The something is the constant, automatic activity of categorizing, narrating, evaluating, instrumentalizing.
You cannot become innocent by trying. But you can notice, again and again, what it's like to be captured. You can practice the return. You can stay with the familiar until it becomes strange. You can describe precisely and let the describing teach you to see. Over time — not weeks, probably years — the grooves of capture get shallower.

Maybe that is all “innocence” finally names: Not a lost garden somewhere behind us, but this capacity that keeps reappearing in the middle of a very complicated life.The child in us is not a memory but a way of attention that can be chosen.

Dedicated to Debi Ji
